items.value: The WTO — the GI Act, 1999 was enacted to meet India's TRIPS obligations
items.reasoning: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 was passed to give effect to Articles 22 to 24 of the TRIPS Agreement, which binds members of the World Trade Organization to provide legal means for protecting geographical indications. The ILO deals with labour standards, the IMF with monetary stability and balance-of-payments support, and UNCTAD is a UN body on trade and development that produces no binding intellectual-property obligations of this kind.

items.value: Statement 3 only — Rajasthan does have iron ore mines; States can auction non-coal mines, and both Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand hold gold deposits
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: since the MMDR (Amendment) Act, 2015 mineral concessions for major minerals other than coal, lignite and atomic minerals are granted by State Governments through auction, so States plainly do have that power. Statement 2 is wrong too, because India's gold resources are distributed across several States including Andhra Pradesh, where the Ramagiri gold field in Anantapur lies, and Jharkhand. Statement 3 is correct: Rajasthan works small iron ore deposits in districts such as Jaipur, Udaipur and Bhilwara, even though it is a minor producer nationally.

items.value: Statement 1 only — BHIM does reach any UPI-enabled account, but the claim that a chip-and-PIN card has four authentication factors is wrong
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: BHIM runs on the Unified Payments Interface, so a user can push money to any account addressed by a UPI ID or by account number and IFSC, across banks. Statement 2 fails on its arithmetic: a chip-and-PIN debit card carries two authentication factors, the card itself, which is something you have, and the PIN, which is something you know — not four. The count for BHIM is also debatable, since device and SIM binding, the app passcode and the UPI PIN are all involved, but statement 2 is already false on the debit-card half alone.

items.value: Bengaluru
items.reasoning: Delhi lies at roughly 77.2 degrees east. Bengaluru at about 77.6 degrees east is barely a third of a degree away, whereas Hyderabad is near 78.5, Nagpur near 79.1 and Pune near 73.9 degrees east. Bengaluru is therefore almost due south of Delhi and is the closest of the four in longitude; Pune, the only option west of Delhi, is the farthest at more than three degrees.

items.value: Child labour
items.reasoning: ILO Convention No. 138 is the Minimum Age Convention of 1973, which sets the minimum age for admission to employment, and Convention No. 182 is the Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention of 1999, which targets slavery, trafficking, forced recruitment, illicit activities and hazardous work by children. India ratified both in June 2017, which is why they were in the news. Neither concerns climate adaptation, food prices or gender parity.

items.value: The statement that a Money Bill concerns appropriation of moneys out of the Contingency Fund — Article 110 says Consolidated Fund
items.reasoning: The question asks which statement is NOT correct. Article 110(1)(d) speaks of the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India, not the Contingency Fund, so option C misstates the provision and is the answer. The other three track the Article faithfully: (a) covers the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax, (c) covers the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund, and (b) covers the regulation of borrowing or the giving of guarantees by the Government of India.

items.value: Statement 1 only — an MLA's vote value varies by State, but every MP's vote, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, has the same value
items.reasoning: The value of an MLA's vote is the State's 1971 population divided by the number of elective seats in its Assembly and then by one thousand, so it differs from State to State — Uttar Pradesh's MLAs carry a far heavier vote than Sikkim's. Statement 2 is wrong because the value of an MP's vote is a single figure obtained by dividing the total value of all MLAs' votes by the total number of elected MPs, and it applies identically to members of both Houses; there is no distinction between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members.

items.value: India's civilian nuclear reactors come under IAEA safeguards
items.reasoning: Under the separation plan that followed the civil nuclear deal, India placed its designated civilian reactors under the IAEA regime, and the Additional Protocol ratified in 2014 supplements that arrangement with further reporting to the Agency. Option B is excluded by the very logic of the separation plan, which keeps military installations outside any international inspection; option C confuses this with the 2008 NSG waiver, which is what opened nuclear commerce to India, and in any case the NSG is a group of supplier states rather than a seller; and option D is false, since NSG membership requires a separate consensus decision that India has not obtained.

items.value: Australia, China, India and Japan
items.reasoning: ASEAN's free trade agreements are with China, Japan, South Korea, India, and Australia and New Zealand jointly under AANZFTA. Australia, China, India and Japan are therefore all free-trade partners, which is option C. Canada and the United States have no free trade agreement with ASEAN as a bloc, which rules out every other option, since A includes Canada, B and D include the USA, and D includes Canada as well.

items.value: Statement 2 only — GACSA membership is voluntary and non-binding; it came out of the 2014 New York summit and India did not create it
items.reasoning: The Global Alliance for Climate-Smart Agriculture was launched at the UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014, not at Paris in 2015, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is its defining feature: GACSA is a voluntary, multi-stakeholder platform whose members take on no binding commitments. Statement 3 is wrong because India stayed out of the alliance, objecting that it blurred the line between mitigation obligations and the food-security concerns of developing-country agriculture, so India was certainly not instrumental in creating it.

items.value: Statement 3 only — rural broadband and public Wi-Fi are Digital India aims; building home-grown internet firms and hosting foreign data centres are not
items.reasoning: Connecting villages through BharatNet and providing Wi-Fi in schools, public places and tourist centres falls squarely within the Broadband Highways and Public Internet Access pillars of the Digital India programme, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 1 is not an aim of the programme, which is about digital infrastructure, governance and services rather than creating Indian rivals to Chinese internet firms. Statement 2 is not among the nine pillars either; requiring foreign companies to localise data centres belongs to later data-protection and payments-data debates, not to the Digital India Plan.

items.value: Pairs 1 and 4 — Aleppo is in Syria and Mazar-i-Sharif in Afghanistan; Kirkuk and Mosul are both in Iraq
items.reasoning: Aleppo is the northern Syrian city devastated in that country's civil war, so pair 1 is right, and Mazar-i-Sharif is the northern Afghan city famous for the Blue Mosque, so pair 4 is right. Both the remaining pairs are wrong for the same reason: Kirkuk, the disputed oil city, and Mosul, retaken from the Islamic State in 2017, are both in Iraq, not in Yemen or Palestine respectively.

items.value: The Governor General
items.reasoning: The Government of India Act, 1935 divided subjects into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists and then vested the residuary power — the authority to decide which legislature could make law on any subject not enumerated — in the Governor General. This is the classic point of contrast with the Constitution of India, where residuary powers rest with Parliament, and it was one of the features the framers deliberately changed.

items.value: Statement 1 only — the Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be a member, but not on dissolution of the Assembly
items.reasoning: Article 179(a) provides that a member holding office as Speaker shall vacate that office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly, so statement 1 states the rule correctly. Statement 2 is excluded by the proviso to the same Article: on a dissolution the Speaker does not vacate office immediately but continues until immediately before the first meeting of the Assembly constituted after the dissolution, so that the office is never vacant.

items.value: If there are no laws, there is no liberty
items.reasoning: Liberal political theory treats law as the condition of liberty rather than its opposite — Locke's formulation is that where there is no law there is no freedom, because without enforceable rules the stronger simply dominate the weaker and no one's freedom is secure. Option A states the crude libertarian inverse, that law and liberty vary in opposite directions, which the tradition rejects; option C describes democratic law-making, a separate question from the law-liberty relation; and option D names a risk of legal instability rather than the relationship itself.

items.value: Both — criminal proceedings against a Governor are barred during the term, and the emoluments cannot be reduced during it
items.reasoning: Article 361(2) states that no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or the Governor of a State in any court during the term of office, which is statement 1. Article 158(4) provides that the emoluments and allowances of the Governor shall not be diminished during his term of office, which is statement 2. Both are express constitutional guarantees, so both statements are correct.

items.value: The Kishangarh school
items.reasoning: Bani Thani is the celebrated eighteenth-century portrait of the Kishangarh school of Rajasthani painting, executed by the court painter Nihal Chand under Raja Savant Singh, and famous for its elongated face, arched eyebrows and exaggerated almond eyes. It is often called the Indian Mona Lisa. The Bundi and Jaipur schools have distinct idioms within Rajasthani painting, and Kangra belongs to the Pahari group.

items.value: An American anti-missile system
items.reasoning: Terminal High Altitude Area Defense is a United States ballistic missile defence system built by Lockheed Martin that intercepts short and medium range missiles in their terminal phase using a hit-to-kill interceptor. It was in the news over its deployment in South Korea, which China objected to strongly. It is neither an Israeli radar, nor India's indigenous programme, which is the two-tier Prithvi and Advanced Air Defence system, nor a Japan-South Korea venture.

items.value: Statements 2 and 4 only — Tyagaraja created new ragas and Annamacharya sang of Venkateshwara; his kritis praise Rama, and the two composers are centuries apart
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong because the overwhelming majority of Tyagaraja's kritis are addressed to Lord Rama, his chosen deity, not to Krishna. Statement 3 is wrong on chronology: Annamacharya belongs to the fifteenth century while Tyagaraja lived from 1767 to 1847, so they are separated by roughly three centuries. Statement 2 is correct, since Tyagaraja is credited with composing in and creating several new ragas, and statement 4 is correct, as Annamacharya's sankirtanas are devoted to Lord Venkateshwara of Tirumala.

items.value: Limitation of powers, equality before law, and liberty and civil rights — but not people's responsibility to the Government
items.reasoning: The rule of law means that public power is bounded by law, that the law applies equally to all including those who govern, and that individual liberty and civil rights are protected against arbitrary state action — so features 1, 2 and 4 all belong. Feature 3 inverts the idea: the rule of law makes the Government answerable to the people and to the law, and a doctrine of the people's responsibility to the Government describes an authoritarian relationship rather than the rule of law.

items.value: Money that a creditor is legally obliged to accept in settlement of a claim
items.reasoning: Legal tender is money that the law compels a creditor to accept in discharge of a debt; refusing it does not keep the debt alive. That is why Reserve Bank notes carry the Governor's promise and why the withdrawal of legal tender status in 2016 mattered so much. Option A misreads the phrase as court fees, option C describes credit instruments such as cheques, which a creditor may lawfully refuse and which are therefore optional money, and option D wrongly restricts legal tender to coin, when notes are legal tender as well.

items.value: The opportunity cost shifts from the consumers of the product to the tax-paying public
items.reasoning: Making a good free to its users does not make it costless: the resources used to produce it still have alternative uses forgone, so an opportunity cost exists and someone bears it. Since the Government finances the provision out of revenue raised from taxpayers, that burden shifts from the people who consume the good to the taxpaying public at large. Options A and B deny that the cost exists or matters, and option D treats the Government as an independent source of resources, whereas its funds come from the taxpayer.

items.value: If poverty and unemployment increase
items.reasoning: This is the standard distinction between economic growth and economic development: a rise in real GNP, even per head, is only an average and can coexist with a worsening distribution. If poverty and unemployment rise alongside output, the gains are accruing to a narrow section and the standard of living of the mass of people has not improved, so the higher figure does not signify development. Sectoral imbalances and a widening trade gap may be problems in themselves, but neither directly contradicts a claim about the level of development in the way rising poverty does.

items.value: Statements 2 and 4 — raising knowledge, skills and capacities of people, which is accumulation of intangible wealth
items.reasoning: Human capital formation is the process of investing in people through education, training, health and skilling so as to raise their knowledge, skill levels and productive capacities, which is exactly statement 2. Because the resulting asset is embodied in human beings and cannot be separated from them, it is intangible wealth, so statement 4 also holds. Statements 1 and 3 describe physical capital formation — accumulating capital goods and tangible wealth — which is a different process from the formation of human capital.

items.value: A high capital-output ratio
items.reasoning: The capital-output ratio measures how much capital must be invested to produce one additional unit of output. When that ratio is high, each rupee of investment yields comparatively little extra output, so even an economy that saves and invests heavily records only a modest rise in production — the Harrod-Domar relation, in which the growth rate equals the saving rate divided by the capital-output ratio, makes this explicit. Weak administration, illiteracy and population density can all impair growth, but the ratio is the direct link between capital formation and output that the question asks about.
